title: How to find a club and join a league in England
seo_title: How to find a table tennis club and league in England
description: How to find a table tennis club near you in England, what a first session is like, how local leagues work and which Table Tennis England membership to get.
summary: Search Table Tennis England's table finder, visit a club, then ask to join one of its league teams. Here is how each step works and what it costs.
key_points: Table Tennis England's table finder lists clubs near you, with filters for beginners, juniors, women and girls, and disability access.
Most local leagues are teams of two or three players, playing weekday evenings from about late September to March.
Clubs enter the teams; you join a team through your club, not by applying to the league yourself.
To play in a local league you need Compete membership of Table Tennis England: £26 for adults in 2026-27.
Club Play membership, for people who only play at their club, is free.
body: To find a club, search Table Tennis England's online table finder, contact the clubs near you and go along to a session. To join a league, ask your club to put you in one of its teams and take out Compete membership of Table Tennis England, which costs £26 for adults in the 2026-27 season. The whole process can take a few weeks.
## Search the table finder
Table Tennis England is the governing body for the sport in England. Its table finder is a map of places to play: type in a town or postcode and choose a radius of five, 10, 15, 20, 25 or 50 miles.

The filters help you narrow it down. Premier club and Associate club pick out clubs affiliated to Table Tennis England. Other filters show outdoor tables, leisure centres, community hubs and bars, and sessions for particular groups: Back to TT for adults returning to the game, Bat & Chat for over-50s, TT Kidz and junior coaching for children, women and girls' sessions, and venues with disability access.
Your local league's website is the other place to look. Most leagues list the clubs that enter teams, with contacts and the nights they play.
## Premier clubs and associate clubs
The two club labels on the map describe a club's affiliation to Table Tennis England, not how good its players are.

An associate club is the entry-level category, which Table Tennis England describes as designed for new and small clubs. A PremierClub is an established club that takes extra support, training and resources from the governing body. Both are covered by Table Tennis England's public liability insurance, which matters if you get hurt or cause damage while playing.
A big club is not always the right choice. A small club with a friendly social night may suit a beginner better than one built around league teams and junior squads.
## Your first visit
Email or ring before you go. Ask which night suits a newcomer, whether you can borrow a bat and what it costs. Clubs set their own fees, and many charge per session at first.

Wear sportswear and indoor trainers with non-marking soles. Expect some practice rallies, a few games against players of different standards and a lot of picking up balls. If you have never played before, our guide to [starting as an adult](/guide/how-to-start-playing-table-tennis.html) covers what to expect.
Try two or three clubs if you can. Ask whether they have teams in the local league and in which divisions, because that tells you whether there is room for a beginner.
## How local leagues work
Most competitive table tennis in England is played in local leagues. Each one is affiliated to Table Tennis England and runs its own divisions, fixtures and rules.

According to Table Tennis England's handbook for league organisers, most leagues play a winter season from around late September to March, with a break at Christmas. Matches are usually on weekday evenings, starting at about 7.15pm or 7.30pm, at one team's club.

Teams are normally two or three players. In the most common three-player format, each player meets each of the three opponents, and many leagues add a doubles to make 10 individual matches. A match night typically finishes between 10pm and 10.30pm. Leagues usually award one point for each individual match won, and the teams with most points top the table.

Bigger leagues have several divisions of around 10 to 14 teams, each playing the others home and away. Teams go up or down at the end of the season, often two at a time. That is good news for newcomers: the bottom division is full of improving and social players.
## How to join a team

You don't apply to a league yourself. Clubs register their teams with the league, and the league registers each player. If you contact a league, its membership secretary will usually pass your details to clubs with a vacancy.

Most clubs will want to see you play first, so they can put you in a team at the right level. Three-player teams usually register at least four players, so a spare place for a reserve is common, and filling in when a regular is away is a gentle way to start.
## Which membership you need

Every player in an affiliated league has to be a member of Table Tennis England, and leagues and tournament organisers are told to refuse entry to anyone who isn't. Leagues usually charge their own registration fee as well.
There are four types of membership for 2026-27. Supporter is free and is for fans. Club Play is also free and adds public liability insurance, for people who play only at their club.

Compete costs £26 for adults, £14 for under-19s and nothing for under-11s. It adds personal accident insurance, local leagues, national rankings and ratings, and entry to local one-star tournaments. Compete Plus costs £49 for adults, £26 for under-19s and nothing for under-11s, and adds all national competitions and the Senior British Clubs Leagues.
For a local league, Compete is the one you need. You join or renew online through Table Tennis England's website. If you live outside England, check its reciprocal membership page first.
## Once you are playing

Your league results count towards a rating, a number that rises when you beat stronger players and falls when you lose to weaker ones. Our guide to [ratings and rankings for club players in England](/guide/table-tennis-england-ratings.html) explains how it works.

Beyond the local league there are tournaments graded by stars, from local one-star events upwards, and national team competitions such as the British Clubs Leagues, including a veterans' league for over-40s. Our guide to [how table tennis is run in England](/guide/table-tennis-england-explained.html) explains how the levels fit together.
## Your next steps

Search the table finder tonight and email two clubs. Before your first league match, read [what makes a serve legal](/guide/legal-serve-rules.html) and [how doubles works](/guide/doubles-rules-explained.html), because you will need both on match night.
